newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebels capture northern town - U.N. sources.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels capture northern town - U.N. sources.

text.p: Rwandan-backed Zairean rebels have extended their control over much of Zaire's eastern border region, capturing Butembo and battling near other towns, U.N. sources said on Friday.

The sources said a resident of Butembo, contacted by radio on Friday, reported rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) had entered on Thursday, pursuing retreating Zairean troops who had looted the town far north of the previous fighting.

The ADFL rebels now control a large swathe of eastern Zaire with the cities of Uvira, Kamanyola, Bukavu and Goma firmly under their control. The U.N. sources said more fighting was taking place further north near the towns of Beni and Bunia,

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has repeatedly said his forces would fight allthe way to the capital Kinshasa to topple ailing strongman Mobutu Sese Seko. Zaire, aid workers and diplomats say Kabila's group is backed by Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army, a charge Rwanda denies.

The fighting coincided with fresh steps toward agreement on a Canadian-led international military intervention to help refugees in Zaire -- and a continuing flow of refugees back across the border to Rwanda that makes intervention less necessary.

A spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said more than 7,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees had returned home on Friday and some 40,000 more were heading for the eastern Zairean town of Sake, near the border, from nearby Minova.

In Bukavu, further south, UNHCR officials said another 1,500 Rwandan Hutus crossed from Zaire on Friday. Officials said they included the first significant number of refugees who had fled southwest to Mwenga when fighting between Zairean rebels and government troops cleared the teeming refugee camps near Bukavu.
"We have had reports of a big group of people at Mwenga, but we believe they will come in groups of about 2,000 to 3,000 a day rather than together," said one official from UNHCR.

About 600,000 Rwandan Hutus have now gone home. But aid officials are not allowed to travel far beyond Bukavu, severly hampering efforts to help thousands of refugees who may still be hiding in the forests of eastern Zaire.

They were allowed to travel 50 kms (30 m) north to Kabamba on Friday to deliver medical supplies to a way-station dealing with refugees who had fled north when the camps emptied. A medical officer in Kabamba said those arriving were in very poor condition and he had five suspected cases of cholera.

Refugees arriving in Bukavu on Friday said former Rwandan army troops and Interahamwe militiamen had threatened to kill those who tried to go home, but hunger and cold in the forests had forced them out.

Privately, some aid officials have said they believe refugees still in Zaire could be the Interahamwe, former Rwandan army and their families. The Interahamwe and their former army allies are chief culprits of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda in which up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed.
The killers fled in 1994 -- along with other Hutus who feared reprisals -- when the Tutsi-dominated Rwanda Patriotic Front rebel group routed them to put an end to the genocide.

They stayed in the refugee camps of eastern Zaire until last month when the Zairean rebels -- made up of various ethnic groups and believed to be supported in part by Rwanda -- took control of large parts of the border area.
